methods.description: On the stated domain, every horizontal line must meet a function graph at most once; one multiple intersection disproves this.
Compare all outputs when every input of the stated finite domain is listed; repeated outputs disprove one-to-one behaviour.
Evaluate two different allowed inputs and show that their outputs are equal.
For the given simple linear rule, assume equal outputs, simplify and show the inputs must be equal.

The source even-function sentence is too broad unless distinct opposite inputs are allowed.

outcomes.independentSolution: The cubic x³ rises through all real inputs, and adding 1 translates it upward without duplicating an output. Every horizontal line meets its full graph once. One-to-one.
outcomes.observation: Used the horizontal line test on the whole unrestricted polynomial graph; the horizontal tangent near the inflection does not create a constant interval.

outcomes.independentSolution: At y=1 the graph of (x−2)² meets x=1 and x=3. Two intersections of one horizontal line disprove the condition. Not one-to-one.
outcomes.observation: The full-domain parabola is correctly rejected; its vertex at (2,0) and y-intercept 4 agree with the graph.

outcomes.independentSolution: The complete domain is {−1,0,1}; its outputs are {3,4,5}, each occurring once. One-to-one on that domain.
outcomes.observation: The wording makes the domain exhaustive, so a table really does suffice. No unlisted inputs are assumed.

outcomes.independentSolution: f(−1)=4=f(1), with −1≠1. This repeated output disproves one-to-one behaviour.
outcomes.observation: All listed inputs still have one output, so this is a function even though it is many-to-one.

outcomes.independentSolution: The full graph of x³+5 rises through every real input. Every horizontal line meets it once; translating the cubic up by 5 changes no intersection count. One-to-one.
outcomes.observation: The full domain is used and cubic coordinate precision must not imply a horizontal segment.

outcomes.independentSolution: f(5)=(5−6)²=1 and f(7)=(7−6)²=1. Inputs 5 and 7 differ but outputs coincide.
outcomes.observation: Both allowed inputs are explicitly evaluated; the dashed graph line y=1 meets them and is not an asymptote.

outcomes.independentSolution: Assume f(a)=f(b). Then 2a−1=2b−1; add 1 to get 2a=2b; divide by nonzero 2 to obtain a=b. Thus equal outputs cannot come from different inputs: one-to-one.
outcomes.observation: The conditional premise is essential and present; elementary linear cancellation is valid for all real inputs.

outcomes.independentSolution: The whole graph of x³+3 rises across all real inputs. Every horizontal line meets it once, so it is one-to-one.
outcomes.observation: Vertical translation does not change the line-test result; no derivative method is needed.

outcomes.independentSolution: The entire stated domain {−1,0,1} has outputs 5,6,7. No output repeats, so the function is one-to-one there.
outcomes.observation: Complete-domain table comparison is sufficient and all three values are distinct.

outcomes.independentSolution: If 5a−4=5b−4, add 4 to obtain 5a=5b, then divide by 5 to obtain a=b. The equal-output condition proves one-to-one behaviour on all real inputs.
outcomes.observation: The current solution includes the conditional premise and intermediate line; no division by an input or zero occurs.

outcomes.independentSolution: Assume f(a)=f(b): 6a−5=6b−5, hence 6a=6b and a=b. Equal outputs require equal inputs, so the function is one-to-one.
outcomes.observation: The constant 5 cancels from both sides and coefficient 6 is nonzero; level and notation are appropriate.

outcomes.independentSolution: f(0)=(0−1)²=1; f(2)=(2−1)²=1. The different inputs 0 and 2 share output 1.
outcomes.observation: This is a valid full-domain repeated-output witness, also shown by the dashed y=1 line. Equality is conceptually necessary.

outcomes.independentSolution: At y=1, (x−4)²=1 has x=3 and x=5. That horizontal line meets the graph twice, so the function is not one-to-one.
outcomes.observation: The vertex (4,0) is retained; the whole real domain contains both sides.

outcomes.independentSolution: The complete table has f(−1)=2 and f(1)=2. Two different inputs give the same output, so it is not one-to-one.
outcomes.observation: The middle output 3 does not remove the repeated 2; it remains a function.

outcomes.independentSolution: Suppose f(a)=f(b). From 4a−3=4b−3, add 3 and divide by 4 to get a=b. Hence no two different real inputs share an output; one-to-one.
outcomes.observation: Elementary linear equal-output algebra is sufficient; the solution correctly states the assumption before equations.

outcomes.independentSolution: f(3)=(3−4)²=1 and f(5)=(5−4)²=1; 3≠5. These are the requested different inputs with the same output.
outcomes.observation: Both arithmetic evaluations are correct; graph and dashed line agree with this witness.

outcomes.independentSolution: At y=1 the graph of (x−6)² meets x=5 and x=7. It fails the horizontal line test and is not one-to-one.
outcomes.observation: Unrestricted polynomial domain includes both branches; a visible finite plotting window is not a domain restriction.

outcomes.independentSolution: Every horizontal line meets the full graph of x³+1 once, so the answer is one-to-one.
outcomes.observation: The function passes both line tests; only the horizontal test answers this stem.
